message.content:
You can likely get closest to “Plastikman / Endel Deeper Focus”‑style, long, stem‑based minimal/dub techno today with **Stable Audio 3.0** (open‑weight models under a permissive commercial license) plus possibly **HeartMuLa** or **Magenta RealTime 2** for custom, locally‑run systems; the cloud‑only models (ElevenLabs Music, Suno v5, Google Lyria 3) give higher polish but are biased toward song‑like structures and short clips, and they generally do not output clean, multi‑hour “non‑song” stems by default.[24][27][3][10][16][17][18][4][7]

Below is a system‑by‑system comparison for your specific use case: *hypnotic, monotone, vocal‑free minimal/dub techno, deep sub, subtle pads, very few events, exported as separate stems, under commercial terms for a paid app*.

---

## 1. ElevenLabs Music API (Music v2)

### (1) Output quality for techno / dub‑techno / ambient‑techno

- ElevenLabs positions **Music v2** as “studio‑grade” multi‑genre generation with control over **genre, mood, structure and duration**.[30][29]  
- A detailed independent review notes that **Music v2 is strongest when the brief demands explicit lyrics and section control**, delivering clearly segmented song forms and high text fidelity.[17][22] That strongly suggests the model is *optimized* for vocal, structured tracks rather than long, structure‑less techno drones.
- There is little 2025–26 public reviewer commentary specifically on *minimal or dub techno*, so evidence for how well it nails that niche is weak. Available reviews focus on pop, hip‑hop, cinematic, and vocal tasks.[17][22]

**Inference:** Expect high general audio quality and good “song” structure, but you would need careful prompting and possibly post‑processing to avoid verse/chorus tendencies for techno‑ish backgrounds.

### (2) Low‑end and kick quality

- ElevenLabs markets the Music API as “high‑quality, original music,” but does not break out low‑end performance.[30][29] Independent reviews likewise emphasize lyrics and structure over detailed spectral analysis.[17]
- No 2025–26 sources explicitly evaluate bass/kick punch for dance music; this is a clear evidence gap.

**Inference:** Likely decent but not tuned for club‑grade sub or the kind of long, stable low‑end you’d expect from Plastikman‑style tracks; you would probably still want external limiting/EQ.

### (3) Long loop‑able, vocal‑free material without “song” structure

- The Music API allows you to set **music_length_ms** to define duration and describes control over **structure** and “vocal or instrumental versions in any genre.”[18][30][28]  
- Reviews show Music v2 easily produced **~90 s** files with clear sections and lyrics when requested.[17][22] There is no public indication that it can generate continuous 30+ minute tracks; in practice this will be segmented into shorter renders that you tile or crossfade.
- You *can* request **instrumental** outputs (i.e., no vocals) via API parameters.[18] But there is no explicit “no song structure” mode; you would likely have to:
  - Prompt for “no vocals, no melody, just monotone minimal techno, no build‑ups”, and  
  - Post‑process into loops yourself (cut, align, crossfade) inside your engine.

### (4) Commercial license

- The Music API is available to **paid subscribers**, and ElevenLabs documentation states that **commercial‑use licensing is included for Starter and higher plans**.[16][17][22][28][29][30]  
- You can integrate it via **ElevenAPI** and embed generation directly into your product.[29][30]  

**Fit:** Legally clean for a subscription app as long as you stay on a paid tier and respect their ToS.

---

## 2. Suno v5 / Suno Studio (v5.0–5.5)

### (1) Output quality for techno / dub‑techno / ambient‑techno

- Suno v5 is described as **“studio‑grade (44.1 kHz) audio”**, with **higher mastering quality**, better separation, and a full DAW‑like environment in **Suno Studio**.[19][25][21][23]  
- A technical review notes that v5 greatly reduces high‑frequency artifacts and improves **frequency separation**, making the stereo field cleaner and more mixable.[20][25]
- This review also remarks that instruments are **richer, better separated, with reduced distortion**, and drums have **more punch**.[25][20]
- However, reviews and Suno’s own marketing are heavily focused on **song‑oriented** content (pop, rock, EDM with vocals). There is little evidence on long‑form minimal/dub techno; most examples are 1–2 verse‑chorus songs.[19][20][25]

**Inference:** For short techno/EDM clips, Suno v5 probably sounds excellent. For extremely sparse, non‑song minimal/dub techno, you’d be pushing the model off its main path.

### (2) Low‑end and kick quality

- Spectral analysis from a 2026 review highlights **“drums have more punch”** and better separation, with fewer “phasey” artifacts and a “lossless feel.”[20][25]  
- This is promising for **kick and bass clarity**, especially when stems are separated, but these tests are not specifically about techno kick design.

**Inference:** Among cloud models, Suno v5 is one of the more promising for **clean, tight low‑end**; you could export stems and re‑shape kicks/sub externally.

### (3) Long loop‑able, vocal‑free material without “song” structure

- Suno v5 generates **song‑length tracks** (typically ~2 minutes per generation) and is tuned for structured songs.[23][21]
- Suno Studio provides **12‑stem separation** and a DAW‑like interface, allowing you to decompose a track into **up to 12 stems** (vocals, bass, drums, keys, etc.) and use them for **“Subtractive Production”**.[20][19]  
- You can mute vocals, cut sections into loops, and rearrange structure manually; but there is no evidence of a “continuous 30 minutes, no song form” mode.
- You can prompt for instrumental tracks and avoid lyrics, though by default Suno likes to generate vocals unless instructed otherwise.

**Inference:** For your use case, you’d generate 1–2 minute techno or ambient‑techno segments, extract stems, and loop in your own engine. Getting completely song‑less, “Endel‑style” monotone output may require heavy curation.

### (4) Commercial licence

- Suno’s ToS (not quoted in the 2025–26 pieces we saw) govern commercial use. Reviewers mention Suno as a tool for content creators and producers; however, details about **embedding generative functionality in a subscription app** are not clearly documented in the sources we have.[19][23]
- Typically, Suno allows commercial use of generated audio under certain plans but may restrict reselling as a service or resyndicating generation capabilities.

**Fit:** Likely usable to *render and ship audio stems*, but you must carefully review and possibly negotiate licensing if your app offers AI generation on demand rather than just static tracks. Evidence here is weak.

---

## 3. Stable Audio 3.0

### (1) Output quality for techno / dub‑techno / ambient‑techno

- Stable Audio 3.0 is a **family of open‑weight models**, with **Small SFX, Small, and Medium** downloadable, and **Large** via API.[24]  
- Stability AI states it is built for **“artistic experimentation”**, with **fully licensed training data**.[24]
- Public reviews for specific *techno/dub‑techno* quality in 2025–26 are sparse; however, the open‑weight nature and focus on general music (with text prompts) make it suitable for experimentation and fine‑tuning. Evidence about genre‑specific fidelity is weak.
- Users commonly use Stable Audio for ambient, cinematic, and electronic soundscapes; that aligns with your minimal/dub‑tech background requirement, but this is more anecdotal (outside the cited docs).

**Inference:** Out‑of‑the‑box, you should get usable techno‑ish or ambient‑techno textures with correct prompting. Being open weights, you could fine‑tune on your own minimal/dub techno corpus to push it toward Plastikman‑like restraint.

### (2) Low‑end and kick quality

- Official docs emphasize general high quality, not specifically bass.[24] There is no formal measurement for low‑end performance in the 3.0 release.
- Since the models are open, you can:
  - Inspect frequency responses,
  - Apply mastering chains,
  - Or fine‑tune on bass‑heavy minimal techno.

**Inference:** Quality is likely acceptable but may require **post‑EQ, multi‑band compression, and careful sample curation** for sub‑bass and kick control.

### (3) Long loop‑able, vocal‑free material without “song” structure

- Stable Audio 3.0’s open weights and **API** allow arbitrary duration control (within model limits) and flexible prompting.[24]
- You can generate **instrumental, non‑vocal content** by prompt, as the model is not inherently lyric‑centric.
- Because you control the entire pipeline locally or through the API, you can:
  - Generate **loopable segments** (e.g., 8–32 bar stems),
  - Align them to a fixed BPM (120–128),
  - Export them as separate bass, pad, percussion, FX layers via either multi‑pass prompting or model editing.

Evidence for explicit “stem output” from Stable Audio 3.0 is weak; most documentation is about full mixes, but the open weights allow you to build your own multi‑pass or multitrack workflow.

### (4) Commercial licence

- Stable Audio 3.0 is covered under the **Stability AI Community License**, which explicitly states you **own your outputs** and **can distribute and commercialize them freely**.[24][27]  
- Open‑weight models (Small, Small SFX, Medium) can be self‑hosted with this license, making them ideal for embedding in a paid subscription app.[24][27]
- Pro/API tiers note that audio generated on **Pro and higher** remains covered under the original license even after cancellation.[26]

**Fit:** Very strong for your use case: open weights, clear commercial rights, self‑hosting allowed.

---

## 4. Google Lyria 3 (via Gemini API)

### (1) Output quality for techno / dub‑techno / ambient‑techno

- Lyria 3 is Google’s **high‑fidelity music generation** line, generating **44.1 kHz stereo** with structural coherence, including **vocals, lyrics, and full instrumental arrangements**.[4][13][5]
- The product page explicitly mentions the ability to generate **minimal techno beats** as one of the use cases.[1][5] That suggests the model has at least some trained capacity for minimal techno, though not necessarily dub‑techno’s aesthetics.
- Lyria 3 Pro is focused on **full‑length songs with verses, choruses, bridges**, while **Lyria 3 Clip** is optimized for **30‑second clips and loops**.[4][7][8]

**Inference:** Audio quality is high; structural understanding is strong for song forms. Minimal techno beats are supported, but the model is not target‑built for long, structureless, monotone techno.

### (2) Low‑end and kick quality

- Official docs focus on high‑fidelity stereo and structural coherence; they do not highlight low‑end behavior.[4][13][14]
- Given Google’s focus on mainstream genres, techno/bass‑specific evaluations are not yet documented in 2025–26 sources.

**Inference:** Likely very clean, but may not automatically produce the ultra‑deep, consistent sub you want without careful prompting and external mastering.

### (3) Long loop‑able, vocal‑free material without “song” structure

- Lyria 3 Clip outputs **30 s clips** designed for loops and previews.[4][7][14] That is directly aligned with using short loops for longer sessions.
- Lyria 3 Pro can create **tracks up to ~3 minutes** with intros, verses, choruses, and bridges.[7][8] That’s the opposite of what you want (song‑like, not monotone), but you could restrict prompts to “no vocals, no chorus, minimal pattern, constant energy” and then manually loop.
- Docs note that tracks can be **instrumental** (no vocals) via prompt.[11][13]  
- There is no indication that Lyria 3 outputs **separate stems**; it appears to export mixed stereo MP3 or WAV.[4][14]

**Inference:** Works nicely for generating 30 s techno‑ish loops you can tile and crossfade. It cannot directly give you multitracks; you’d need separate generations or external stem separation.

### (4) Commercial licence

- Lyria 3 is exposed via **Gemini / Google AI Studio / Enterprise Agent Platform**.[4][7][14]  
- Enterprise documentation frames it as usable inside products, but detailed commercial and redistribution terms are handled via Google Cloud/Gemini licensing, not fully spelled out in the technical docs.
- Typically, Google grants usage rights to generated content but may restrict model misuse or disallow reselling their generation capabilities as an API.

**Fit:** Strong for pre‑rendered content in an app if you’re under a paid Gemini/enterprise license, weaker if you want fully local or open‑weight deployment.

---

## 5. Magenta RealTime 2 (MRT2, open weights, Apple Silicon)

### (1) Output quality for techno / dub‑techno / ambient‑techno

- Magenta RealTime 2 is described as a **state‑of‑the‑art open‑weights model for real‑time music generation**, with **2.4B parameter Base** and **230M Small**.[3][6][10][15]
- It is the open‑weights cousin of **Lyria RealTime**, which powers Google’s live music features (e.g., Music FX DJ, real‑time APIs).[12] This implies mainstream‑level quality.
- Public commentary emphasises **real‑time synthesis, low latency (~40 ms)** and live control rather than genre specifics.[3][10][12] There is little explicit feedback about minimal/dub techno quality; evidence is weak on this niche.

**Inference:** Excellent for live, controllable generative music; you can steer it into techno/dub‑techno with MIDI and text controls, but you may need to design your own prompt/control schemes.

### (2) Low‑end and kick quality

- Technical write‑ups focus on latency, context window (~20 s), model size, and Apple Silicon performance.[3][10][12][15] Bass quality is not discussed.
- As a live, streaming model, you can route its outputs through your own **EQ, compression, saturation**, and even layer in dedicated sample‑based kicks to guarantee club‑style low‑end.

**Inference:** You shouldn’t rely on MRT2 alone for perfect techno kicks; instead, treat it as a generator of mid‑range and atmosphere, with your own low‑end chain.

### (3) Long loop‑able, vocal‑free material without “song” structure

- MRT2 is specifically designed for **real‑time streaming**, generating audio faster than playback on Apple Silicon (Small can stream on any M‑series Mac, Base needs higher‑end chips).[3][10][12][15]  
- It has an effective receptive field of ~**20 seconds**.[10] That means it doesn’t “remember” structure beyond that horizon, which naturally **discourages long song‑like arcs** and instead favours ongoing, evolving patterns—ideal for **focus music and monotone textures**.
- With real‑time **MIDI, text, and audio controls**, you can:
  - Fix BPM externally,
  - Hold a constant pattern,
  - Avoid lyrics entirely by not feeding text for vocals.

**Inference:** Very strong fit for streaming **endless, non‑song, evolving minimal techno** as a background generator. You can record stems live or stream them directly.

### (4) Commercial licence

- MRT2 is **open weights**, published under Google’s open‑weights terms via HuggingFace.[3][6][10][15] Exact legal text is not in the snippets, but it is positioned similarly to other open‑weights models (non‑copyleft).
- You can run it **locally** on Apple Silicon via MLX/C++.[3][6][10][12][15] This makes it attractive for an app that wants fully internal generation, though you must inspect the actual licence to confirm redistribution/embedded use.

**Fit:** Technically ideal: open weights, Apple Silicon‑ready, real‑time, controllable. Legal details need verification but are likely favorable.
